tts: Open any social app, and within a minute, someone will show you their abs, their breakfast, and their discount code. Fitness influencers are everywhere. And from the outside, it looks like a dream job: work out, film it, get rich. But how does that money actually work? Who pays them, how much, and why do some of them end up selling companies for billions, while most never earn enough to quit their day job? In this video, we'll climb the fitness influencer money ladder, step by step, from the very bottom to the very top. And at the end, we'll look at the uncomfortable truth behind all those perfect bodies. Let's warm up.

First, why fitness? Because it's almost the perfect kind of content. It never runs out: there's a new workout every day, a new recipe, a new challenge. It's visual: muscles, sweat, and the most powerful format on the internet, the before and after. It's personal: people don't just watch, they follow someone's journey for months, and that creates a strange kind of friendship. And it's useful. A workout video isn't just entertainment, it's something you can do with them, right now, in your living room. Put those four things together, and you get content that people come back to every single day.

Then twenty twenty happened. Gyms around the world closed almost overnight, and millions of people suddenly had to work out at home, with nothing but a phone. In Britain, trainer Joe Wicks started a free daily workout for kids called PE with Joe. On one of the first days, nearly a million households tuned in live at the same time, a YouTube record. Fitness apps and home equipment sold out. And a huge number of people discovered they could follow a coach through a screen. When the gyms reopened, that habit didn't go away. At the same time, short vertical video exploded on TikTok, Reels and Shorts, and a thirty-second workout clip became the perfect thing to scroll past and save for later.

So, step one of the money ladder: views. This is where most people think influencers get rich. They don't. On YouTube, long videos in fitness can earn a few dollars per thousand views, depending on the country of the audience. Shorts earn far, far less, often just a few cents per thousand. And on Instagram, Reels don't pay creators directly for views at all anymore. That means a million views can bring a lot of attention, but often less money than people imagine. Views aren't the paycheck. They're the shop window.

Step two: brand deals and promo codes. This is where the shop window starts to pay. A brand sends leggings, protein or pre-workout, and pays the influencer to show it. Often, the influencer also gets a personal discount code, and a cut of every sale made with it. Sometimes it's a small percentage, sometimes much more, especially with apps and subscriptions. The British clothing brand Gymshark built itself this way. Its young founder, Ben Francis, started out by sending clothes to fitness YouTubers and paying some of them small monthly fees to wear them. Their fans bought the look. In twenty twenty, an investment firm bought a stake that valued Gymshark at around a billion pounds. One rule to know: in many countries, including the United States, influencers are legally required to clearly label paid posts as ads.

Step three: selling their own knowledge. Programs, meal plans, coaching and apps. This is where the business model gets really interesting. A twelve-week workout program is filmed once, but it can be sold thousands of times, and every extra copy costs almost nothing to deliver. Online coaching pays more per client, but it's limited by time: one coach can only answer so many messages. That's why many successful influencers move from personal coaching to group programs and apps, where one piece of work can serve a hundred thousand people at once. The followers they built in step one become the customers they sell to in step three.

The most famous example is Kayla Itsines, a personal trainer from Australia. She started by posting before-and-after photos of her clients on Instagram, then sold a workout guide as a simple PDF. That guide became an app called Sweat, with millions of users. In twenty twenty-one, at the peak of the home-workout boom, Sweat was sold to the American fitness company iFIT, in a deal widely reported as worth around four hundred million dollars, though later filings suggested the real figure was lower. Then the boom cooled down, iFIT changed strategy, and in twenty twenty-three, Kayla and her co-founder bought the app back for a fraction of that price. Same app, very different value, all depending on timing.

Step four, the top of the ladder: their own brand. Instead of earning a commission on someone else's product, the influencer owns the product. Clothing, supplements, energy drinks, protein bars. Here, an audience becomes something extremely valuable, because a new brand normally has to pay a fortune to get noticed, and an influencer already has millions of people paying attention for free. The biggest example so far: fitness influencer Katy Hearn co-founded a brand of energy drinks and supplements called Alani Nu. In twenty twenty-five, the energy drink company Celsius agreed to buy it for one point eight billion dollars. That's the jump from being paid for a post, to owning the company the posts are about.

But here's what the highlight reels don't show: at every step of this ladder, the work grows. A serious fitness creator isn't just training. They're filming, editing, writing captions, answering hundreds of comments and messages, negotiating with brands, and posting almost every day, because the algorithm rewards consistency and punishes breaks. Many of the bigger names have whole teams behind them: video editors, managers, nutrition experts and customer support. And their bodies are part of the product, which is a strange kind of pressure: if you get injured, gain weight, or simply age, your business can suffer. Burnout is common. Some of the most successful creators say the hardest part isn't the workouts at all. It's never being allowed to switch off.

Now, the uncomfortable truth. For every Kayla or Katy, there are thousands of fitness creators who never make real money. Estimates of the creator economy suggest that only a few percent of creators, around four percent by some counts, make more than a hundred thousand dollars a year. Most earn little or nothing. We just never see them, because the algorithm shows us the winners. And even the winners show us a filtered version: perfect lighting, flexing at the right angle, sometimes editing. Some sell supplements with bold promises and little evidence. So when you see a fitness influencer, it helps to ask one simple question: what are they selling, and who benefits if I believe this?

So, let's put the ladder together. Step one, views: attention, but not much money. Step two, brand deals and promo codes: the first real income. Step three, their own programs and apps: knowledge sold thousands of times. Step four, their own brand: owning the product, and sometimes selling it for billions. And under every step is the same foundation: trust. Followers buy from people they feel they know. That's the real business of a fitness influencer. They're not really selling workouts. They're selling trust, one post at a time. And if you've ever bought something because someone on your phone said it worked for them, you're part of this story too.
